client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time I walk past her favorite coffee shop — the one we used to go to every Sunday — I just get hit with this wave of sadness that I can't shake. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because it's not like anything can actually change what happened.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — those sudden waves of grief that hit in familiar places can be especially painful, and it makes complete sense that the coffee shop carries so much weight for you. You're right that nothing can change what happened, and I want you to know that's not what we're here to do; instead, this space is about helping you carry that grief a little more gently. I'm curious — when you say you're not sure talking will help, is there a part of you that still wanted to try anyway?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess, yeah, there is a part of me that wanted to try, otherwise I wouldn't be here. But it's hard to explain — it almost feels like talking about her too much might make it worse, like I'll just end up more upset and then have to go back to my regular life feeling raw. I don't know if that makes sense, but it's like I'm scared of opening something I won't be able to close again.
therapist: That makes complete sense, and it actually takes a lot of courage to show up anyway even when part of you is afraid of what might come up. That fear of "opening something you can't close" is really common in grief — it's your mind trying to protect you from being overwhelmed. I'm wondering, though, has there ever been a time when you let yourself feel something difficult and found that you actually did make it through to the other side?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very loud, very rapid speech

client: I mean, yeah, I guess when my dog died a few years ago I was really devastated, and eventually I did get through it. But this feels different, bigger somehow — my grandmother was such a constant in my life, every single Sunday for as long as I can remember, and I'm not sure that comparison really holds up. It's like losing a dog is sad, but losing her feels like losing a whole piece of who I am.
therapist: What you're describing — losing a piece of who you are — is such a profound way to put it, and it sounds like your grandmother was woven into your very sense of self, not just your routine. I notice as you're talking about her, there's something that feels almost quiet and far away in how you're carrying this, like the weight of it might be even deeper than the words can quite reach. Can you tell me a little more about what it feels like inside when you say she was "a constant" — what did that consistency mean to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: She was just... always there, you know? No matter what was going on in my life — good weeks, bad weeks, times when I felt completely lost — Sunday mornings with her were this guaranteed anchor. And now without that, the weeks just kind of blur together and I feel unmoored, like I don't quite know where I belong anymore.
therapist: That word "unmoored" is really striking — it captures something so real about what happens when we lose a relationship that was essentially a compass for us. It sounds like those Sunday mornings weren't just time together, they were a place where you could bring all the versions of yourself — the lost ones, the happy ones — and feel held. I'm curious, when you imagine your weeks now, is there any small moment or person that offers even a flicker of that same sense of anchor, or does it feel completely absent right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, it feels pretty absent most of the time. There are a couple of friends I could probably reach out to, but I always talk myself out of it because I don't want to burden them with my grief, especially this far out from the funeral when everyone else seems to have moved on. It's like there's this pressure to already be okay, and admitting I'm still struggling feels like I'm doing something wrong.
therapist: That belief — that you're "doing something wrong" by still grieving — is such a painful and unfair burden to carry on top of the loss itself, and I want to gently challenge it: grief doesn't follow a timeline that other people's comfort sets for you. What strikes me is that you mentioned friends you *could* reach out to, which tells me part of you is still looking for that anchor. I wonder, what do you imagine your grandmother would have said if you told her you were holding back from asking for support because you didn't want to be a burden?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: She would have told me off for that, honestly — she had no patience for people shrinking themselves unnecessarily, and she'd probably say something like "don't be ridiculous, your friends love you." But knowing what she would have said and actually believing it myself feel like two completely different things, and I'm not sure that reframe is enough to make me pick up the phone. It's easier to imagine her saying it than to actually trust that my friends would feel the same way.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you know her so well you can still hear her voice on this — that's a testament to how deeply she knew and accepted you. And you're putting your finger on something important: there's a gap between understanding something intellectually and actually feeling it in your bones, and that gap is real and worth taking seriously. I'm curious — when you imagine reaching out to a friend and them responding warmly, what gets in the way of letting yourself believe that could actually happen?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think part of me is waiting for the moment when they get tired of it, when I can see in their response that they're a little relieved when I change the subject. It's happened before — not with grief specifically, but just in general, where I've shared something heavy and the other person kind of deflects or goes quiet, and that sticks with me more than all the times people have actually shown up. So I guess I've built this case in my head that reaching out will end in that kind of quiet rejection, even if the evidence isn't really all there.
therapist: You've just described something really important — that your mind has learned to hold onto the moments of disconnection more tightly than the moments of being truly met, and that's not a character flaw, it's actually a very human way of trying to protect yourself from being hurt again. And yet there's something almost tender in the way you're describing this, like part of you is tired of carrying that case you've built against reaching out. I'm wondering — if you were to look at the full evidence, not just the moments of deflection but also the times people *have* shown up for you, what would that picture actually look like?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: If I'm being honest, the picture is more balanced than the story I tell myself — there have been friends who've sat with me through hard things, who've texted to check in, who've shown up in ways I probably don't give them enough credit for. But even acknowledging that feels uncomfortable, like I'm dismantling something I've built for a reason, and I'm not sure I trust myself not to just go back to the same pattern the next time I'm about to reach out. It's like knowing the evidence doesn't automatically change the feeling in my chest when I'm actually staring at my phone.
therapist: What you're describing — knowing the truth but not yet *feeling* it — is actually at the heart of so much of the work in therapy, and it's a really honest and self-aware place to be. That feeling in your chest when you're staring at your phone is where the real change happens, not just in the thinking but in slowly, gently practicing doing it differently even when it's uncomfortable. I'm wondering if we could think together about what the smallest possible version of reaching out might look like — something low-stakes enough that it doesn't trigger that full alarm in your chest, but still a tiny step toward letting someone in.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Maybe something like sending a text that doesn't fully expose how I'm feeling — like asking a friend if they want to grab coffee without making it this big emotional declaration. But even that feels a little dishonest, like I'm using a normal social thing as a cover for actually needing something, and I worry that if they say no or they're busy, it'll just confirm that story in my head all over again. I guess the smallest step sounds manageable in theory, but I can already feel myself looking for reasons it won't work.
therapist: It's really telling that you came up with a genuinely good idea and then, almost in the same breath, started building the case against it — that pattern of anticipating failure before you've even tried is worth noticing, because it's the same protective instinct that's been keeping you isolated. And I'd gently push back on the idea that asking a friend for coffee is dishonest — needing connection *is* the real thing, and coffee is just a gentle, human way of reaching toward it. What if a "no" or a "I'm busy" didn't have to be the end of the story — is there a way we could think about how you'd want to respond to yourself in that moment, rather than letting it become proof of the story?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think what you're saying makes sense, but I honestly don't know what I would say to myself in that moment — my instinct is just to shut down and take it as confirmation, and I'm not sure I have a kinder voice ready to step in. It's like you're asking me to have a resource I'm not sure I've built yet. Maybe that's actually part of what's missing, not just the reaching out but having something inside that can hold me steady when it doesn't go perfectly.
therapist: What you just named is actually a really significant insight — that the missing piece isn't just about reaching out, but about building an internal steadiness that can catch you when things don't go perfectly. That kind of inner voice doesn't appear overnight, but the fact that you can already identify its absence tells me you're starting to know what you're looking for. I wonder if your grandmother's voice — the one that told you not to shrink yourself — might actually be a place to start borrowing from, while your own kinder voice is still finding its footing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
